clue.text: Ambassador visiting Caribbean island with 27's mother

indicators.note: an envoy visiting a place sits right beside it, so the two pieces are simply joined

parts.note: HE, His Excellency, is the form of address for an ambassador
the largest island in the Caribbean

explanation.surface: A diplomat travels to Cuba accompanied by the mother of someone mentioned elsewhere in the puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 27 across is HECTOR, the Trojan hero; the definition sends you to his family in Homer's Iliad.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend Hecuba, queen of Troy, was the wife of Priam and mother of Hector.

clue.text: Murder in institution probed by one with police?

indicators.note: something probed has another thing pushed inside it, so the first word encloses the rest

parts.note: a home is a residential institution, such as a care home
the Roman numeral for one
the Criminal Investigation Department, Britain's plain-clothes detective branch

explanation.surface: A killing inside some institution is being looked into by an officer and the police.
explanation.definitionFit: Homicide is the legal term for the killing of one person by another, a synonym of murder.

clue.text: Terribly cruel act seen in black and white

indicators.note: something done terribly is botched and mangled, so these letters come out in a new order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An atrocity is recorded in a black-and-white photograph or newspaper report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In black and white' suggests print or film; here it means stark and unambiguous.
explanation.definitionFit: Something set out in black and white is plain and definite, which is what clear-cut means.

clue.text: British also developed a missile

indicators.note: a thing that has developed has changed its form, so the letters change their order

parts.note: standard abbreviation for British
the letters of this word rearranged

explanation.surface: Britain has also built a new missile.
explanation.definitionFit: Bolas are weighted cords thrown to tangle an animal's legs, a thrown weapon and so a missile.

clue.text: In the dark I allow doctor to come in

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the doctor is asked to step inside, so that piece goes within the word for allow

parts.note: to grant is to allow
Dr No, the villain of the James Bond film

explanation.surface: Someone without information lets a doctor into the house.
explanation.walkthrough: The doctor here is not the usual crossword medic but the title villain of the Bond film Dr No.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in the dark is an idiom for lacking knowledge, so it means uninformed.

clue.text: RAF officer in class with ship's commander

parts.note: a group is a class or category
the officer in command of a ship

explanation.surface: An air force officer sits in a class alongside a naval captain.
explanation.definitionFit: Group captain is a Royal Air Force rank, equivalent to a naval captain or army colonel.

clue.text: Oxford University athlete, awfully shabby

indicators.note: something done awfully is done badly, so these letters come out jumbled

parts.note: abbreviation for Oxford University
the letters of this word rearranged

explanation.surface: A university sportsman is looking terribly scruffy.
explanation.definitionFit: Out at heel is an idiom for wearing worn shoes, hence shabby and down at heel.

clue.text: Almost all of state capital is imposing

indicators.note: almost all means everything except a final scrap, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: Augusta is the capital of the US state of Maine

explanation.surface: Nearly every part of a state's capital city is grand and impressive.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital is American, Augusta in Maine (also Georgia's golf town); the adjective august is stressed on its second syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: August as an adjective means majestic and inspiring respect, which is what imposing describes.

clue.text: Ancient city in Egypt he besieged

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of words that follows, spanning their boundaries

parts.note: found across the end of Egypt, all of he and the start of besieged

explanation.surface: A man laid siege to an old city in Egypt.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is literally true, which is the trick: the city is in Egypt in both senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Thebes was the great capital of ancient Egypt on the Nile, now Luxor.

clue.text: Even bits of nuts, lime, bananas, may make up a breakfast dish

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange
even bits are the second and fourth letters, those in even-numbered positions

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of the word
taken as written, to be mixed with the pair before

explanation.surface: A list of ingredients, nuts, lime and bananas, for a morning bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: Bananas looks like a third ingredient in the list; it is the crazy-making signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Muesli is a Swiss mix of oats, nuts and fruit eaten for breakfast.

clue.text: Rapidly cut film sequence involving upper-class Veronese family

indicators.note: to involve is to take in, so the first word wraps around the next

parts.note: a montage is a sequence of quickly edited shots
U is the old label for upper-class usage

explanation.surface: A film montage features a posh family from Verona.
explanation.definitionFit: The Montagues are Romeo's family in Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet, set in Verona.

clue.text: Pass duke speedily

parts.note: to hand over is to pass
duke is slang for a fist, as in put up your dukes

explanation.surface: A duke is quickly passed by, as if on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: Duke reads as a nobleman; here it is boxing slang for a fist.
explanation.definitionFit: Hand over fist is an idiom for doing something, especially making money, quickly and in large amounts.

clue.text: One may not get a fair deal from me

definitions.text: One may not get a fair deal from me

parts.words: One may not get a fair deal from me
parts.note: surface reading: a trader or official warning you against them
setter's reading: a deal of playing cards, rigged by a cheat at the table

explanation.walkthrough: Deal sounds like a business bargain; it is the dealing of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheat at card games deals dishonestly, so opponents never receive an honest hand.

clue.text: Having original of Sunflowers in gallery causes a sensation

indicators.note: the gallery is having something within it, holding it inside

parts.note: the Tate, London's national art gallery

indicators.note: the original of a word is its very first letter

parts.note: first letter of the painting's name

explanation.surface: Showing Van Gogh's Sunflowers in an art gallery creates a stir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Causes a sensation' reads as one phrase of excitement; split it, and a sensation alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Taste is one of the five senses, a sensation perceived on the tongue.

clue.text: Cheat merchant after large drink

indicators.note: one word comes after the other, so it is placed second in the line

parts.note: a double is a large measure of spirits
a dealer is a merchant or trader

explanation.surface: A trader orders a stiff drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A double-dealer acts two ways at once, deceiving people, so is a cheat.

clue.text: There may be sensationalism in lady's initial undress, I suspect

indicators.note: suspect means dubious and not quite right, so the letters are disordered
an initial is the opening letter of a word

parts.note: first letter of lady
these letters reshuffled

explanation.surface: A tabloid speculates that a woman's first striptease will be a scandal.
explanation.definitionFit: Lurid means shocking and gaudy, so luridness is the sensational quality of a story.

clue.text: Gloomy, unused actors

definitions.meaning: first meaning: dull and cloudy, as a sky
second meaning, split in two: performers cast beyond the number needed, so left spare

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning splits the word into OVER and CAST: actors left unused because too many were cast.
explanation.definitionFit: An overcast sky is grey and gloomy; read in two parts, it is surplus members of a cast.

clue.text: Fools brought before stipendiary, primarily, or judge

indicators.note: one thing brought before another stands in front of it in the line

parts.note: asses are fools

indicators.note: primarily means at first, so only the opening letter is used

parts.note: first letter of stipendiary
taken as written

explanation.surface: Idiots are hauled up in front of a stipendiary magistrate or a judge.
explanation.walkthrough: A stipendiary is a paid magistrate in British courts, so the courtroom picture hides the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An assessor evaluates and gives a verdict, and to judge is to evaluate.

clue.text: Common soldier is in play

parts.note: a private is the lowest army rank
to be is to exist, so is gives lives

explanation.surface: An ordinary soldier is acting in a stage play.
explanation.definitionFit: Private Lives is a 1930 comedy by Noël Coward, so it is an example of a play.

clue.text: Greek character one of three adults ejected from dance

indicators.note: something ejected is thrown out, so that letter is removed from the dance

parts.note: the lambada is a Brazilian dance
A stands for adult, and the dance contains three of them

explanation.surface: A Greek man is one of three grown-ups thrown out of a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: The dance has three As and any one may go; dropping the third gives the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lambda is the eleventh letter of the Greek alphabet, the equivalent of L.

clue.text: Whack barrier round front of pub

parts.note: a wall is a barrier
O is round in shape

indicators.note: the front of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of pub

explanation.surface: Someone hits a wall near the entrance of a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A wallop is a heavy blow, and as a verb it means to hit hard, a synonym of whack.

clue.text: Prize in a lottery rejected

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a thing rejected is turned back, so that word is read from the end

parts.note: a lottery is a draw

explanation.surface: A lottery winner turns down their prize.
explanation.definitionFit: An award is a prize given in recognition of merit or achievement.

clue.text: Strengthen control by coercion

parts.note: to rein is to control
force is coercion

explanation.surface: An authoritarian tightens their grip through intimidation.
explanation.definitionFit: To reinforce is to make stronger by adding support, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Celebrity pots first of reds in a game of snooker

indicators.note: to pot is to sink something into a pocket, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: fame is celebrity

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: first letter of reds

explanation.surface: A star player sinks red balls during a snooker match.
explanation.walkthrough: In snooker, reds are the fifteen red balls potted first, so the whole surface is a scene from the game.
explanation.definitionFit: A frame is a single game in a snooker match, played from the opening break to the last ball.

clue.text: Newspaper round at home?

parts.note: a round of ammunition is a bullet
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: A paper delivery round from home.
explanation.walkthrough: Round suggests a paper round; it is a round of ammunition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bulletin is a news report or periodical, and many newspapers carry the name.

clue.text: Badger, tough short brute

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: hard means tough
an ass is a beast of burden, a brute

explanation.surface: A badger is described as a hardy, stocky beast.
explanation.walkthrough: Badger is the verb, not the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: To badger someone is to pester them persistently, a synonym of harass.

clue.text: Oat-pipes, remarkably suitable

indicators.note: something remarkable is out of the ordinary, so the letters fall out of their ordinary order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Rustic pipes made from oat stalks are surprisingly fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Apposite means apt and relevant to the situation, so suitable.

clue.text: Bully boy

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to intimidate with talk
second meaning: a male given name

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read as a playground thug, but they are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: To hector is to browbeat, after the swaggering Trojan hero, and Hector is also a boy's name.
